topic: Fundamentals of Vector Spaces: Span, Dependence, and Bases

sections.title: Prerequisite Review: The Vector Concept
sections.content: Define a vector as a directed line segment from the origin. Visualize 2D vectors as arrows. Introduce 'Linear Combination' as scaling and adding arrows together.
sections.example: Imagine a robot arm moving in a 2D plane: scaling two basic motor inputs (v1, v2) to reach any coordinate (x, y).

sections.title: The Concept of Span: 'Reachability'
sections.content: Define Span as the set of all possible points reachable by taking linear combinations of a set of vectors. Visualize this as the 'shadow' or 'area' cast by the vectors.
sections.example: Two non-parallel vectors in 2D 'span' the entire plane; one vector only spans a single line.

sections.title: Linear Dependence: The 'Redundant' Vector
sections.content: Explain Linear Dependence: A set is dependent if one vector can be expressed as a combination of others (i.e., it doesn't add 'new' dimensions). Visualize this as a third vector lying flat on the plane formed by the first two.
sections.example: If you have three people pulling a wagon in the same direction, the third person is 'linearly dependent'—their effort doesn't change the path.

sections.title: Bases: The Minimalist Framework
sections.content: Define a Basis as the 'Goldilocks' set: enough vectors to span the space, but no redundancy (linearly independent). This acts as a coordinate system for the space.
sections.example: The standard basis vectors i=(1,0) and j=(0,1) are the most efficient 'map' for a 2D grid.

sections.title: Summary & Synthesis
sections.content: Recap the logical progression: Linear Combinations build Span; too many vectors create Dependence; the minimal set required to span is a Basis.
sections.example: Think of a basis as the 'keys' on a piano: they are independent notes that, when combined, can span the entire musical range of the instrument.
